paragraphs: Language models need to represent relationships among words while handling large vocabularies. The paper describes a practical tension: flexible models often rely on local optimization, while more manageable alternatives impose strong restrictions on the distributions they can represent. It proposes a Markov random field language model that can use context extending across longer stretches of text.

The learning method takes a variational approach to optimizing likelihood. It also uses symmetries within the model to simplify the computation. These symmetries are central to the contribution: the authors exploit shared structure in the problem to make a demanding learning objective more manageable. They describe their approach as global-likelihood optimization with time independent of corpus size.

The paper demonstrates computational efficiency in both language modeling and part-of-speech tagging. These applications show how the proposed learning method can support different language tasks. The contribution is a step toward combining richer contextual dependencies with efficient likelihood optimization, rather than a claim that vocabulary-related difficulties have been completely resolved.
icml-2015-a-fast-variational-approach-fo.tldr: A variational method exploits model symmetries to efficiently learn Markov random field language models with long-range context.

paragraphs: Zero-shot learning asks a model to recognize a concept from its description, without requiring training examples of that concept. This paper proposes a particularly simple approach to that problem. Its central contribution is that a compact learning rule can perform strongly despite the complexity usually associated with connecting observed features to descriptions of unfamiliar classes.

The method belongs to a broader framework connecting features, attributes, and classes through two linear layers. The upper layer receives its weights from the environment instead of learning them from the training data. This supplied information provides the link to class descriptions. The authors also analyze generalization by treating the framework as a domain adaptation problem and deriving a learning bound.

Experiments on three standard real datasets report significantly better performance than the state of the art on all three, with an improvement ratio reaching 17%. The result supports the value of this simple construction in the tested settings. The theoretical contribution complements those experiments by examining how this family of methods can generalize.
icml-2015-an-embarrassingly-simple-appro.tldr: A simple two-layer linear framework recognizes unseen classes from descriptions and outperforms prior approaches on three datasets.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to connect short descriptions in ordinary language with snippets of source code. It builds probabilistic models that represent both kinds of information jointly. The motivation is to bring together statistical modeling of code and the idea of learning relationships between two different forms of data, previously explored for images and language.

The authors evaluate the models in two retrieval directions. In one, a natural language query is used to retrieve a relevant code snippet. In the other, a code query retrieves a natural language description. The paper calls this second task source code captioning, but the demonstrated task is retrieval of descriptions rather than a claim about unrestricted generation of new explanations.

The experiments indicate that joint modeling is promising for these tasks. They also show that representing the structure of source code helps retrieval. That finding gives the work a specific methodological message: the organization of code contributes useful information when connecting programs to language, beyond simply placing the two kinds of data in a shared modeling problem.
icml-2015-bimodal-modelling-of-source-co.tldr: Joint probabilistic models connect code snippets with natural language, with code structure helping retrieval in both directions.

paragraphs: Binary embedding compresses high-dimensional points into strings of bits while retaining information about their distances. This paper studies points on a sphere and asks how many bits are needed to recover their geodesic distances with a uniform error tolerance. It addresses both the fundamental storage requirement and the computational cost of constructing the representations.

For embeddings chosen independently of the points, the authors prove a lower bound proportional to log N divided by δ squared, where N is the number of points and δ controls distortion. They establish a similar bound for data-dependent embeddings into Hamming distance. Their proposed algorithm matches this bit requirement and runs in O(p log p) time when log N is much smaller than δ times the square root of p.

For larger log N, the stated runtime is somewhat worse, so the fastest guarantee is conditional. The paper also analyzes more general point sets, including infinite ones. Experiments on synthetic and real data support the theoretical findings, connecting efficient construction with provably optimal bit complexity.
icml-2015-binary-embedding-fundamental-l.tldr: The paper proves binary embedding limits and gives an algorithm with optimal bit complexity and conditionally near-linear runtime.

paragraphs: Celeste models optical telescope images by connecting observed pixel intensities to hidden properties of stars and galaxies. Its generative approach describes how those underlying celestial objects could produce the images. Inference then works in the opposite direction, using the images to estimate the properties of the objects that generated them.

Each pixel intensity follows a Poisson distribution whose rate depends on the latent properties of celestial sources. Important source properties are also treated as random quantities. Their prior distributions draw on scientific information constructed from large ancillary datasets. This creates a probabilistic connection between prior knowledge about celestial objects and the evidence contained in the telescope images.

The authors introduce a variational procedure for carrying out inference in this model. They check the approach on synthetic images and apply it to images from a major sky survey. In that survey evaluation, it exceeds the existing state-of-the-art method for locating celestial bodies and measuring their colors. These findings support the practical value of combining a generative image model with scientifically informed priors.
icml-2015-celeste-variational-inference-.tldr: Celeste combines a generative telescope-image model with variational inference to improve celestial object localization and color measurement.

paragraphs: This paper considers sequential learning when observing the average reward of a group of actions costs less than observing one action individually. Monitoring and surveillance motivate the setting: a group of actions can correspond to a geographical area. The learner must therefore consider both the rewards it accumulates and the expense of gathering information.

The key assumption is that rewards vary smoothly over a graph connecting neighboring actions. Under this structure, observations of groups can help the learner make useful decisions while controlling sensing costs. The proposed CheapUCB algorithm matches regret guarantees of known algorithms for the setting while also providing a linear cost advantage. Regret measures the cumulative reward lost relative to the comparison used in the learning problem.

The analysis additionally proves a regret lower bound of order square root of dT for spectral bandits on a class of graphs with effective dimension d. This result identifies a theoretical barrier within that graph class. Together, the contributions show how graph structure can support cheaper observation without sacrificing the stated regret guarantees.
icml-2015-cheap-bandits-f7180ec44d.tldr: CheapUCB uses group observations and graph-smooth rewards to reduce sensing costs while matching existing regret guarantees.

paragraphs: Large neural networks can demand more storage than memory-constrained mobile devices can provide. HashedNets addresses this mismatch by reducing the number of distinct parameters stored in a network. The approach exploits redundancy among connection weights, allowing many connections to reuse a parameter while retaining the network's collection of connections.

A low-cost hash function assigns connection weights to groups called buckets. Every connection assigned to the same bucket uses the same parameter value. The shared values are trained with standard backpropagation, so learning adjusts them within the weight-sharing arrangement. The hashing procedure determines which connections share values without introducing additional memory overhead for that procedure.

Experiments on several benchmark datasets show substantial reductions in storage requirements while mostly preserving generalization performance. The qualification matters: the result is strong compression with much of the predictive performance retained, rather than a guarantee of identical performance. The paper's contribution is a simple architecture in which parameter sharing is built into training and directly addresses the cost of storing neural networks.
icml-2015-compressing-neural-networks-wi.tldr: HashedNets compresses neural networks by hashing connections into shared parameters, substantially reducing storage while mostly preserving generalization.

paragraphs: Combining several classifiers can improve decision making, but a fusion center needs to know how much confidence to place in each classifier. That creates a difficulty when individual accuracies are unknown. In applications without true labels, supervised training of the fusion center may also be unavailable, leaving the system without a direct way to learn which decisions deserve more weight.

The paper proposes an unsupervised scheme that jointly estimates classifier accuracies and combines their decisions. Its distinctive feature is that accuracy depends on data context. Instead of treating a classifier's reliability as a single fixed property, the method estimates reliability as a function of the context in which the classifier makes its decision.

Joint estimation and detection connect these two problems: assessing local decision makers and forming an overall decision. Numerical results report a dramatic improvement over the state-of-the-art approaches considered. The finding supports context-sensitive, unsupervised fusion in the evaluated setting, particularly where unknown classifier accuracy and unavailable labels make the usual supervised design difficult.
icml-2015-context-based-unsupervised-dat.tldr: An unsupervised fusion method jointly estimates context-dependent classifier reliability and combines decisions, reporting substantial numerical improvements.

paragraphs: Correlation clustering groups graph nodes according to positive and negative relationships. Positive edges favor placing their endpoints together, while negative edges favor separation. This paper studies the problem when edge weights arrive as a stream of updates, requiring algorithms to work with a changing graph while using limited memory.

The authors develop linear-sketch data structures that can measure the quality of a proposed partition. They combine these compact summaries with sampling and convex programming to construct approximation algorithms. The resulting methods run in polynomial time and use O(n polylog n) space for a graph with n nodes. Achieving that memory bound requires addressing the optimization steps themselves, since standard linear and semidefinite formulations do not obviously fit within it.

The paper therefore also supplies space-efficient convex programming methods and ways to reduce sampling adaptivity. These are supporting contributions needed to make the streaming approach work as a whole. The improved resource bounds also have relevance beyond streams, including offline computation organized through MapReduce.
icml-2015-correlation-clustering-in-data.tldr: Compact graph sketches, sampling, and space-efficient optimization enable correlation clustering approximations in dynamic streams.

paragraphs: Flexible probability models can describe complicated data, but their usefulness also depends on whether learning and computation remain manageable. This paper develops a generative approach intended to combine that flexibility with tractable sampling, inference, and probability evaluation. Its organizing idea comes from nonequilibrium statistical physics.

The method first applies a gradual forward diffusion process that repeatedly destroys structure in the data distribution. It then learns a reverse process that restores structure. The sequence of transformations is central: the generative model is built through many stages of reversing the gradual destruction, allowing a deep model to represent complex data while retaining manageable computations.

The authors state that this construction supports rapid learning, sampling, and probability evaluation in models with thousands of layers or time steps. It also permits computation of conditional and posterior probabilities under the learned model. These capabilities matter because the model serves both generation and probabilistic inference. An open-source reference implementation accompanies the work, providing an implementation of the proposed algorithm.
icml-2015-deep-unsupervised-learning-usi.tldr: Learning to reverse a gradual diffusion process produces flexible deep generative models with tractable sampling and probabilistic inference.

paragraphs: Dirichlet process mixture models allow their complexity to change as more data become available. This flexibility makes them useful for clustering, density estimation, and topic modeling, but computational demands have limited their use on large datasets. The paper addresses that gap with a distributed inference algorithm for both Dirichlet process and hierarchical Dirichlet process mixtures.

The algorithm uses a variant of slice sampling. It avoids a predetermined truncation, preserving an unbiased stationary distribution for the sampling algorithm. This property concerns the distribution targeted by the sampler; it does not mean that any finite collection of samples is automatically exact. The authors implement parallelism both among local threads and across separate machines.

Experiments on image and text data compare the method with existing inference algorithms. The reported results combine state-of-the-art accuracy with strong scalability up to 512 cores. The contribution is therefore both statistical and computational: the method retains the untruncated sampling target while making inference practical across substantially more computing resources.
icml-2015-distributed-inference-for-diri.tldr: A distributed slice sampler scales DP and HDP mixture inference to 512 cores without predetermined truncation.

paragraphs: Rank aggregation combines ranking information into an overall ordering. This paper studies a version in which the available information is a probability distribution over all possible rankings. That shift changes how desirable properties of an aggregation rule should be expressed, since the input is distributional rather than presented directly as a collection of individual rankings.

The authors translate familiar social welfare axioms into this setting and give them quantitative characterizations. Making the axioms quantitative helps clarify their meaning and simplifies proofs of some impossibility theorems. More significantly, it creates natural ways to relax the requirements. Under those relaxed requirements, the authors show how to avoid certain celebrated impossibility results in social choice theory.

The paper also completely characterizes positional scoring rules with respect to its axioms and establishes an optimality result for Borda Count in a particular sense. That qualification is essential: it is an optimality statement within the proposed analysis, not universal superiority over every ranking method. The work connects distributional information with precisely adjustable aggregation requirements.
icml-2015-distributional-rank-aggregatio.tldr: Distributional rank aggregation makes social choice axioms quantitative, enabling relaxations and a qualified optimality result for Borda Count.

paragraphs: Stacking recurrent neural network layers creates a deeper sequence model, but the arrangement of communication between layers also matters. This paper introduces gated-feedback RNNs, which allow upper recurrent layers to send signals to lower layers. A global gating unit for each pair of layers controls these exchanges, extending the usual stacked architecture.

The gates adapt to the current input and the previous hidden states. Consequently, the model can change how strongly layers interact as it processes a sequence. The architecture is evaluated with several recurrent unit types, including tanh units, long short-term memory units, and gated recurrent units. This examines the feedback design across different underlying recurrent mechanisms.

On character-level language modeling and Python program evaluation, the reported experiments show improvements over conventional deep stacked RNN approaches. The authors suggest that learned gates let layers adapt to different timescales and patterns of interaction, including top-down communication. This is a proposed explanation for the empirical gains, rather than an independently established account of why every improvement occurs.
icml-2015-gated-feedback-recurrent-neura.tldr: Adaptive gates control feedback between recurrent layers, improving performance on character language modeling and Python program evaluation.

paragraphs: Hyperparameters shape how a learning algorithm trains, but tuning them is difficult when gradients of validation performance are unavailable. This paper computes exact gradients of cross-validation performance with respect to hyperparameters by differentiating backward through the entire training procedure. Training itself becomes the sequence of computations through which the validation objective is traced.

The mechanism is exact reversal of stochastic gradient descent with momentum. By reversing those training dynamics and chaining derivatives backward, the method connects changes in training choices to changes in cross-validation performance. This gives a gradient-based route to adjusting the procedure that produced the trained model, in addition to adjusting the model's ordinary learned weights.

The resulting gradients allow optimization of thousands of hyperparameters. The examples include learning-rate and momentum schedules, initialization distributions, detailed regularization schemes, and neural network architectures. The contribution is the ability to obtain and use these gradients across a large hyperparameter space. Exact differentiation describes the gradient computation; it does not by itself assert that hyperparameter optimization reaches a global optimum.
icml-2015-gradient-based-hyperparameter-.tldr: Exactly reversing momentum-based training enables gradients of validation performance for optimizing thousands of hyperparameters.

paragraphs: Structured prediction assigns multiple labels jointly, accounting for relationships among them. A common approach scores a complete labeling by adding terms that each depend on a pair of labels. The paper asks how to explain the practical success of heuristic inference methods for such problems through a theoretical analysis of achievable prediction error.

Its focus is expected Hamming error, which counts incorrect labels rather than treating every imperfect overall labeling as equally wrong. The authors study the smallest achievable expected error, with particular attention to two-dimensional grid graphs. These graphs are relevant to machine vision, where the relationships between prediction locations often have a grid structure.

The main results provide tight upper and lower bounds on this error and a polynomial-time algorithm that achieves the bound. Matching an achievable error level to a theoretical lower bound identifies what efficient inference can accomplish in the studied problems. This addresses predictive accuracy directly and supplies a theoretical perspective on why useful structured predictions can be obtained efficiently.
icml-2015-how-hard-is-inference-for-stru.tldr: Tight prediction-error bounds and an efficient algorithm clarify achievable inference accuracy, especially on two-dimensional grids.

paragraphs: Non-negative matrix factorization represents data through combinations of non-negative components, making it useful for admixture problems. Its non-convex optimization landscape makes general correctness guarantees difficult. Earlier guaranteed methods focused on separable factorizations, a restricted class. This paper introduces subset-separability to extend the range of factorizations that can be studied with guarantees.

The authors show that subset-separability is a necessary condition for a factorization to be unique or have minimum volume. Necessity does not make it a sufficient condition for either property. They then develop Face-Intersect, an algorithm that efficiently solves subset-separable NMF under additional natural conditions, and prove robustness to small amounts of noise.

Simulations explore the algorithm's behavior, including settings where it empirically outperforms state-of-the-art methods. These results accompany a conditional theoretical guarantee rather than establishing a solution to every NMF problem. The main advance is a broader structural framework for provably correct factorization, together with an algorithm and a small-noise robustness result within that framework.
icml-2015-intersecting-faces-non-negativ.tldr: Subset-separability broadens guaranteed NMF, with Face-Intersect providing efficient recovery under stated conditions and robustness to small noise.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to infer scale-free network structure from data, a problem relevant to social and biological networks. It uses a Gaussian graphical model regularized by a prior on node degrees. The goal is to encourage the desired overall network structure while using information about individual nodes during inference.

The proposed prior combines a preference for the global degree distribution with estimates of each node's degree and the relative strengths of that node's edges. A ranking-based procedure updates degree estimates dynamically. This makes the prior responsive to the developing network estimate, but also creates a challenging optimization problem. The authors introduce an alternating direction method of multipliers procedure to solve it.

On synthetic and real data, the method produces scale-free networks and correctly predicts many more edges than the compared scale-free, hub-inducing, and l1 priors. The finding matters because obtaining the desired global degree pattern is only part of network recovery. The experiments also assess whether the inferred connections themselves are correct.
icml-2015-learning-scale-free-networks-b.tldr: A dynamically updated node-degree prior improves scale-free network inference and edge recovery in synthetic and real-data experiments.

paragraphs: Word embeddings often learn relationships from which words occur together, while giving limited attention to ordering and word structure. This paper proposes a neural language model that includes both word order and character order in its representations. The approach brings information about sequences of words and the internal arrangement of characters into the embedding model.

The model produces several vector spaces with meaningful internal structure. The authors support this claim through word-analogy performance, reporting 85.8% on a recent task and a 58% error-margin improvement over the best published syntactic analogy scores. These findings provide task-specific evidence that the representations capture useful relationships, particularly those evaluated through syntactic analogies.

The paper also introduces parallel training methods to support very large models. Its most prominent scaling result is training a skip-gram network with 160 billion parameters overnight on three multicore CPUs, described as 14 times larger than the previous largest neural network. The work therefore combines an order-aware representation approach with methods for making large-scale training computationally feasible.
icml-2015-modeling-order-in-neural-word-.tldr: Order-aware word and character representations achieve strong analogy results, alongside parallel methods for training extremely large embedding networks.

paragraphs: Predicting a time series becomes harder when some past observations are missing. This paper treats the task as online learning: the learner makes predictions as the sequence unfolds and seeks to minimize prediction error. It develops an efficient method based on an autoregressive model, which uses earlier values to predict later ones.

A central feature is that the method does not assume a particular structure in the missing data or a particular mechanism generating the time series. This avoids making the learning approach depend on a specified pattern of missing observations. The theoretical comparison is instead made against the best autoregressive predictor chosen after seeing the sequence.

The authors show that their algorithm's performance asymptotically approaches that hindsight benchmark. This is a long-run comparison with a particular predictor class, rather than a claim of perfect predictions or superiority to every forecasting method. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data corroborate the theory, supporting an online approach to autoregressive prediction when observations are incomplete.
icml-2015-online-time-series-prediction-.tldr: An efficient online predictor handles missing observations and asymptotically approaches the best autoregressive predictor in hindsight.

paragraphs: Image captioning requires connecting visual content with a sentence that describes it. This paper proposes a simple model organized around phrases, with particular attention to sentence syntax. Its approach separates finding language relevant to an image from assembling that language into a descriptive sentence.

A previously trained convolutional neural network supplies the image representation. A purely linear model maps that representation into a shared space for images and descriptive phrases. Given a new image, the system uses this space to infer relevant phrases. A simple language model then uses statistics of sentence descriptions to turn the inferred phrases into an appropriate caption.

The authors evaluate the approach on Flickr30k and Microsoft COCO, reporting results comparable to state-of-the-art models despite a considerably simpler construction. The significance is that useful captioning performance can emerge from a relatively direct combination of visual representations, phrase matching, and sentence statistics. The stated result is comparable performance on those datasets, rather than an assertion that simplicity always yields better captions.
icml-2015-phrase-based-image-captioning-.tldr: A linear image-to-phrase mapping and simple language model produce captions competitive with more complex approaches on two datasets.

paragraphs: Finding the most probable joint configuration in a graphical model is a difficult inference problem. Particle-based max-product methods approximate continuous possibilities using sampled candidates, but earlier diverse particle max-product work focused on tree structures. Motivated by protein side-chain prediction, this paper extends the approach to models containing loops.

The authors modify the objective for selecting diverse particles and prove that it is submodular. This property supports an efficient greedy selection algorithm with rigorous optimality guarantees and associated max-marginal error bounds. They also incorporate tree-reweighted max-product variants, enabling verification of global maximum-probability recovery in many models. That verification capability is qualified; it is not a guarantee of global recovery for every loopy model.

The resulting method is implemented in a general-purpose Matlab library for a broad range of pairwise graphical models. Evaluation includes optical flow benchmarks and protein side-chain prediction. For the latter, the method achieves better prediction accuracy than baseline algorithms from Rosetta. The work combines a broader continuous-inference method with guarantees for key approximation and verification steps.
icml-2015-proteins-particles-and-pseudo-.tldr: Submodular particle selection extends continuous max-product inference to loopy models and improves protein side-chain prediction in experiments.

paragraphs: Measurements can reflect both a quantity of scientific interest and the influence of confounding factors. This paper addresses the task of removing those confounding effects so that the underlying, unobserved quantity can be reconstructed. Its astronomy application concerns systematic errors in the search for exoplanets, where separating the desired signal from other influences is the motivating problem.

The proposed method is called half-sibling regression. It is inspired by causal inference research using additive noise models. This places the reconstruction problem in a causal framework: the method is concerned with the effects of confounders on observations and with recovering the latent quantity after accounting for those effects.

The authors provide a theoretical justification for the method and illustrate its potential through a challenging astronomy application. These are complementary contributions: the theory supports the proposed reconstruction approach, while the application shows its relevance to a scientific measurement problem. The stated finding is an illustration of potential, so the contribution should be understood as a justified method with a motivating demonstration rather than a claim of universal confounder removal.
icml-2015-removing-systematic-errors-for.tldr: Half-sibling regression uses a causally motivated approach to remove confounding effects and reconstruct a latent scientific signal.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization uses a relatively inexpensive surrogate model to guide evaluations of an expensive objective. Its effectiveness depends on representing a distribution over possible functions accurately. Gaussian processes commonly fill this role, but their cubic scaling with the number of observations becomes a bottleneck when optimization requires many evaluations or substantial parallelism.

This paper explores neural networks as an alternative basis for that function distribution. The method uses adaptive basis function regression with a neural network providing the parametric form. The authors report performance competitive with state-of-the-art Gaussian-process approaches while scaling linearly, rather than cubically, with the amount of data.

The improved scaling enables a degree of parallel optimization the authors describe as previously intractable. They apply it to large-scale hyperparameter searches for convolutional networks on object recognition tasks and neural language models for image captioning, rapidly finding competitive models. The contribution connects surrogate-model design directly to the practical ability to conduct larger, more parallel searches over expensive learning systems.
icml-2015-scalable-bayesian-optimization.tldr: Neural-network-based surrogates make Bayesian optimization scale linearly with observations while remaining competitive with Gaussian-process methods.

paragraphs: The paper develops a Gaussian process model for Bayesian inference on Poisson point processes. These models concern observed event locations, and the computational challenge grows with the number of observations. The proposed approach aims to retain a nonparametric model while making inference practical for substantially larger datasets.

The model avoids dividing the domain into a grid and avoids introducing latent thinning points. Its stated computational complexity is O(nk squared), with k much smaller than the number of observations n, compared with cubic scaling for competing models. The authors also propose a Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler to carry out inference under the model.

On synthetic and real data, the method is reported to be faster and more accurate than the competing approaches, with less correlation among generated samples. These results address both computational expense and sampling behavior. The authors additionally demonstrate handling dataset sizes not previously considered by alternative methods, supporting the claim that the formulation expands the practical scale of point-process inference.
icml-2015-scalable-nonparametric-bayesia.tldr: A scalable Gaussian-process point-process model avoids gridding and thinning points while improving runtime, accuracy, and sampling behavior in experiments.

paragraphs: Persistent homology studies the shape of data across multiple scales. When observations form a large point cloud drawn from an unknown distribution, computing it directly can become prohibitively expensive. The difficulty comes from the combinatorial growth of the existing algorithms, which makes increasing sample size costly even when more observations could provide useful information.

The paper proposes computing persistent homology on several smaller subsamples and combining the resulting estimates. This changes the computational strategy from one large calculation to a collection of smaller calculations followed by aggregation. The central question is whether this reduction in workload can preserve meaningful information about the shape represented by the full dataset.

The authors study the risk of two estimators and prove that the subsampling approach retains stable topological information while greatly reducing computational complexity. The guarantee concerns stable information carried by the estimates, rather than exact reproduction of every feature from a full-data computation. The contribution is a statistically analyzed route to making topological data analysis more computationally manageable.
icml-2015-subsampling-methods-for-persis.tldr: Combining persistent-homology estimates from subsamples preserves stable topological information while greatly reducing computational complexity.
